speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are just a few words I should like to say on this motion which has been placed before us by the President of the Privy Council. We have no objection to the motion, which calls for a two-week recess beginning at six o'clock tomorrow night, but I think that the President of the Privy Council at some point ought to take us into his confidence and tell us what is involved, particularly since we are coming back on a Thursday rather than on a Monday as is usually the case following an Easter break. In view of the fact that Thursday, April 13, is the day when President Nixon arrives in Ottawa, it seems only fair that we should be told what plans the government has in mind, particularly for the House of Commons.
My other comment, Mr. Speaker, also arises out of the proposal for a slightly extended recess at this time. With the speculation abroad about a general election, it seems to me that the government might also take us into its confidence in that matter. I realize that if I were to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) directly-and that is the way you like us to put questions-when the election is going to be held, he probably would not be as definite as some of us have been. But, Mr. Speaker, I remind the government that on certain occasions in the past when a general election has been more or less certain the government has told the House what its plans were so that the business of the House could be arranged for the last week or two in an orderly fashion. It seems to me, if the government is not prepared to make such a statement with
respect to this motion, that it should, when we come back after the Easter recess, make a clear statement as early as possible and tell us what the actual position is. If the election is going to be put off until next fall or next year, let the government say so categorically. But if it is planning to hold the election at the end of June, I suggest we ought to be told so that the business of the House can be dealt with in an orderly fashion during the last week or ten days that we are here.
You guys just don't know when the election will be. You cannot make up your minds.

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MATTER INVOLVING ANTON SOBOTKA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are fully aware that there is constant work and vigilance in Canada on security matters and that at the same time it is not customary to comment on these matters or on this work. Indeed, the success of security work requires this restraint.
There has been recent speculation concerning a security matter associated with the name Anton Sobotka. This speculation is based on a fictional account which itself was based in part on real facts, and which formed a part of training material for our security work.
I should reassure hon. members that, while the case is interesting, it bears little resemblance to the colourful speculation about it. Indeed, the espionage depicted is espionage at a low level, and the case is one of effective counter-espionage work in discovering it rather than a defection.
Having said that, I hope that hon. members will agree with the ordinary procedure of avoiding comment on security matters. In the ordinary course the Leader of the Opposition is briefed on security matters. In this case, as Acting Solicitor General, I would be glad to discuss in full detail with the leaders of the opposition parties the training material to which I have referred.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MATTER INVOLVING ANTON SOBOTKA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT ON MATTER INVOLVING ANTON SOBOTKA
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Munro that Bill C-170, to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last evening I was making some remarks with regard to criticisms concerning Bill C-170, an act to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Order, please. In fairness to the hon. member who has the floor, I wonder if the conferences and consultations between hon. members might take place behind the curtains.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, last evening I was voicing my criticisms of Bill C-170, which is an act to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children. I said that my three main grounds of criticism were, first, that in the act we replace the principle of universality with the principle of selectivity; second, that the act will stigmatize and categorize people earning certain incomes; and third, that since the act is so complex, it will lead to confusion, misunderstanding and resentment.
Some hon. members here no doubt will recall when legislation concerning family allowances was introduced back in 1944. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said that three members only who now sit in parliament were present when the late

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
Mackenzie King introduced the family allowances legislation. No doubt they recall the election of 1945, in which the Liberals were swept back to power through the political footwork of the late Mackenzie King. He introduced the family allowances legislation. I am sure that some here will recall the remarks made by the late George Drew concerning family allowances. He said that they were iniquitous. The Conservative party had a hard time living down the label which attached to it as a result of comments like that concerning family allowances. May I also remind hon. members that all members of all parties unanimously voted in favour of the family allowances legislation in 1944. I think it is fair to say that the prospect of family allowances was one of the determining factors that persuaded many of the people in Newfoundland that their province ought to enter confederation.
Between 1944 and the present, there have been no changes in the categories of people who are eligible for family allowances or amounts paid under that legislation, despite sharp increases in living costs between 1944 and 1972. Probably, because the legislation has not been changed, it has been criticized. Some people say that it has lost its effectiveness.
Acting on criticisms, the government prepared a white paper entitled Income Security for Canadians which was tabled on November 30, 1970. This dealt with two areas involving social security: First, old age security concerning senior citizens; second, guaranteed income security for families; in other words, family allowances. I remind hon. members that the white paper was tabled on November 30, 1970. On the following day, the government introduced legislation concerning old age security payments. Under that legislation the government increased the basic old age security payment by 42 cents. Cost of living increments were not to apply to the basic old age security payment. Also, for the first time, the government introduced the guaranteed income supplement for old age pensioners, and the 2 per cent cost of living escalation was to apply to the pension and supplement, when paid together. Mr. Speaker, there we saw the first departure from the principle of universality concerning old age security pensions. The government adopted the principle of selectivity.
May I remind hon. members that, beer use the government abandoned the principle of universality and adopted the principle of selectivity, many old age pensioners have experienced difficulty in determining their incomes, largely because of the complexity of the regulations. They have experienced frustration in anticipating their incomes for the following year and determining the amount to which they will be entitled. Also, unnecessary resentment has developed among senior citizens, since one group gets only the basic old age security payment and the other group gets the old age security payment plus the guaranteed income supplement. Many say that their basic old age security payment of $80 is a poor reward for their hard work in contributing to the development of Canada. At 65, if they possess certain assets or a certain income, they are deprived of any government pension payment larger than the basic old age security pension of $80 per month.
It can be said that in adopting the principle of selectivity as opposed to universality, the government has led to

divisiveness within the country. Bill C-170 adopts the principle of selectivity instead of universality, the principle formerly adhered to. Last Friday, the minister attempted to show that certain organizations across the country support the changes in the legislation proposed by the government. We must be thankful for hon. members like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Not only is he the father of procedure in this House-I should say, the expert on procedure-but he is also a man of great patience. He has tremendous knowledge in this field. He corrected the minister when the minister tried to leave the impression that certain organizations supported the legislation. In particular, I am thinking of the Canadian Council on Social Development and the Canadian Labour Congress.
May I put on record again what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said concerning the attitude of the Canadian Council on Social Development towards this legislation. On page 1140 of Hansard for March 24, 1972, the hon. member for Winnipeg No th Centre read a recommendation of the Canadian Council on Social Development, as follows:
The council believes that:
Family allowances should be universal, paid to all families with dependent children as a social right thus avoiding divisiveness among families and any element of stigma. The present program has this feature but FISP would eliminate it.
It took the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to set the minister straight with regard to the position of the Canadian Labour Council. It has been said, and it should be repeated, that the approach with regard to the problem as contained in the proposals in the white paper should have been referred to a committee of this House for study.
The minister attempted to answer the criticism on Friday by saying that the Senate Committee on Poverty had studied the question in depth. A matter of this importance should have been referred to the appropriate committee of this House. I am sure hon. members would not have objected if the committee had been comprised of members of the House of Commons and the other place. This opportunity for study has been denied because the white paper was tabled in November, 1970 and to date there has not been any reference to the committee. If we are to ascertain the attitudes and criticisms of organizations across this country, the white paper should have been, and still should be, referred to the appropriate committee so there would be an input from the many concerned people who are expert in the field in order to obtain the best possible legislation.
The change from the principle of universality to selectivity will create a divisiveness that is not worthy of pursuit. It will create a divisiveness between persons getting family allowances and those who are not. It will divide us into haves and have-nots. It will make the not-so-poor pay for the poor. If this is so, we should hesitate to proceed on a principle that will create divisiveness. I respectfully submit that the change from universality to selectivity will obtain that result.
The second point of criticism is that the act stigmatizes and categorizes people on low income. Poverty is a relative term these days. I can recall many members, myself
March 28, 1972

included, pleading poverty at the time the salaries of members of the House of Commons were increased. I am sure it can be said that poverty is a very relative term. We can have poverty which is a denial or absence of the basic living needs of people and cultural deprivement or spiritual impoverishment can be included in the general definition of poverty.
The Economic Council of Canada made a study of poverty. It found that the basic minimum income for a single person living in Canada today would be approximately $2,000 in order to keep him above the poverty level. The basic minimum income for a married couple would be between $3,500 and $4,000. The astounding fact is that 20 per cent of all Canadians live below the poverty level. This is why we have to look at this problem with all the seriousness and concern we can give to it. I have said that it will stigmatize people according to their income and divide us into the haves and have-nots. With regard to family benefits, it will make the not-so-poor pay for the poor.
One of the proud facts of being a Canadian is that regardless of nationality, race, linguistic or cultural differences, we categorize people as Canadians. We create unity amongst all people living in Canada. In fact, one of the clarion calls of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the last election campaign was unity. I respectfully submit that the programs we are developing and devising will not create unity in Canada, but disunity because of the divisiveness that will be created and the stigmatization that will be imposed on people according to their income. Surely, no man should be judged by the income he obtains. He should be judged on the basis that he is a Canadian and that he has a basic right to employment, education, medicare and all those things that make us essentially Canadian. To develop legislation which divides rather than unites is not worthy of this government.
It can be easily said that this may be an attempt by the government to deal with the problem of poverty by giving people with low incomes certain benefits which will close the gap of poverty. This is a very small step. The major step we as Canadians have to take is legislation to provide full employment, housing and medicare. These are the things that will attack poverty. The measure providing family allowances, even though it is a very minimal step, will do very little to close the large gap that exists between the income levels of Canadians today. Not only am I opposed to the legislation on the ground that it imposes selectivity rather than universality, but it imposes a stigmatization on poor people. This brings me to my third point.
The act is so complex that it will lead to confusion, misunderstanding and resentment. Mr. Justice Hart, the chairman of the Law Reform Commission, said last week that the laws of Canada should be so expressed that they are understood by all Canadians. I am sure all members will agree with that proposition. This government has brought forth legislation so complex that it makes it very difficult for any Canadian to understand it fully. Need I remind hon. members of the Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement legislation? I also remind hon. members of the tax bill that we recently passed. We now have the family allowances bill which is
Family Income Security Plan
very complex. I have had an opportunity to look at the bill. I have found it very difficult to follow. However, I have received some encouragement.
With regard to the complexity of the bill, the minister said last Friday, as recorded at page 1133 of Hansard, and I quote:
The white paper suggested that benefits might be reduced by $1 per month per child for each extra $500 of income. We find after discussion with various people that a provision of these lines might act as a disincentive. The plan, therefore, calls for an adjustment of 30 cents for each $100 extra of income.
He then set forth the principle. He said:
To make benefits selective, an income floor of $4,500 is established below which full benefits will be paid and above which benefits will be reduced as income increases. The income floor is raised by an additional $500 for each extra child in the family. The ceiling of cut-off point for benefits depends upon the number of children, their ages and the reduction rate.
That is the basis on which the allowances will be paid. He also said and I quote:
The scope of the new FISP proposals is such that it replaces both family allowances and youth allowances. The plan takes into account the number and age of children in a family. As far as coverage is concerned, all children under 18 are covered. As far as benefits are concerned, I have already indicated what they will be. In connection with the deduction as income rises, I have indicated that benefits per child are reduced in one-child families with incomes above $4,500 a year and in two-child families with income above $5,000 a year. The income floor rises by $500 for each extra child. The plan introduces a reduction rate of 33 cents per child per month for each extra $100 of income, or $1.65 for each $500, above the floor set for families at that size.
Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that it takes almost half a page to set forth the criteria? The minister went on to say:
The maximum income in one-child families beyond which no benefits are paid is $10,560 if the child is between the ages of 12 and 17 and $9,045 if the child is younger than 12. In the case of two-child families the figures are $11,060 and $9,545. For three-child families, if the children are aged between 12 and 17-and there is a mixture here between 12 and 17 and under 12-the figures are $11,560 and $10,045, and so on by $500 intervals. I repeat that FISP benefits are not counted as taxable income.
Then, Mr. Speaker, in a moment of graciousness, he said:
The House will perhaps be interested to hear what is counted as income in the determination of benefits. The income of a person includes all items of income subject to tax, plus unemployment insurance, scholarships and bursaries, adult training allowances and Canada Pension Plan and Quebec Pension Plan, orphans and dependant children's benefits. It does not include social allowances based on a means or income test.
Further on, he says:
Options will be permitted allowing the substitution of an estimate of income in the calendar year of 12 times the average monthly income in the remainder of the current calendar year instead of being based on the previous year's income as is the usual case.
Mr. Speaker, it has taken me about five minutes to set forth the criteria on the basis of which family benefits will be paid. Under the 1944 act, the criterion was simple. If a person was of a certain age and fell into a certain category, a definite amount was obtained. This was understood by all Canadians. Under the new system it is almost impossible to determine whether a family qualifies or not,

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
whether the income, details of which are submitted, is sufficient to qualify one for benefits. I have never seen such a hodge-podge of rules and criteria. There is no question we shall encounter many difficulties, not only in relation to the act itself but in relation to the regulations which will follow.
There has been an outcry across Canada against the system of calculation of income which is being adopted in connection with UIC payments. Without doubt there will be similar protests concerning the method the minister proposes to use to determine whether young people qualify under this legislation and how much they are entitled to receive. Proposals of this type are not worthy of the government. One of the first objects we should seek to realize is clarity when it comes to legislation. The legislation before us will create division as a result of the change from the principle of universality to the principle of selectivity. It will have the effect of stigmatizing people whose incomes are low. It will introduce unnecessary complexity into the question of determining who should qualify for benefit.
It is for these reasons I have set forth my criticism of this bill. I hope the government will decide not to act at this time but, rather, they will agree to refer the white paper which was tabled in 1970 to the appropriate committee so that it might be studied in depth, enabling a bill to be presented which would be understood by all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am tremendously interested in this legislation, not because I have ever benefited from family allowances personally but because of the circumstances connected with the bringing into effect by the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King of the family allowances legislation in 1944 and 1945. I think I can speak dispassionately upon the subject of social security because I am one who has not accepted the old age pension, believing that the contribution I had made was not in keeping with what the return would be if I were to collect it. I can, therefore, speak with some objectivity concerning the bill before us. We note there have been a great number of changes in the present bill as compared with the bill introduced last session under the number C-264.
I look back to 1944 and 1945. I listened the other day to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) telling us what took place at that time. He pointed out that only three members of the present House were here at that time the vote took place. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was a member at that time, as I recall it, but left shortly for the pastures and power in the Province of Saskatchewan. These things bring to mind the attitude of the Conservative party at the time. Personally, I supported from the very beginning the principle of family allowances. There were some who said it was socialism. I was able to indicate that I did not believe socialism and social security to be synonymous, as is often claimed, or, indeed, on a par with that, that Liberalism and liberty were synonymous.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Both these myths have been dissipated in the intervening years.
I wonder why the changes have been made in the bill. I shall be interested to hear the minister. As it happens, there are only two ministers in the House at the present time, an indication of the degradation of this institution as a place in which, as a result of argument, changes can be brought about. In the days I have just been recalling, Mr. King was present a great deal of the time, despite the fact we were in the midst of a war.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: He is probably present now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
He was present and he listened to arguments made by members of the opposition with respect and regard. If they were fruitful in content, they became embodied in the legislation. But that is all over now. The legislation is fixed up in the East Block by civil servants and that is all there is to it. This is the reason parliament is falling into desuetude. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has shown his disregard for parliament over and over again. This to me is one of those things which represents a situation that is dangerous to Canada and its freedom. For when this institution dies, freedom dies.
I go back to the bill that was introduced on September 13 last. I should like to know from the minister what kind of political legerdemain has been going on. Is it the result of representations made by the provinces? Why these changes? I intend to refer to a most striking example of how the constitution can be degraded, with the Prime Minister of this country passing it off, as he did. I refer to a matter that strikes at the very heart of the institution of parliament and of the legislature of the province of Quebec, or any province, namely that the oath of allegiance shall be removed without there being a constitutional amendment.
When the legislation was originally introduced it was gone into in an exceptionally masterful way by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard). The last hon. member to speak analyzed this legislation in a way that showed he had given a great deal of study to the subject, yet there was no minister here to listen. He made a worthy contribution, and when a worthy contribution is made, from whatever part of the House, it should receive the attention of all parts of the House.
The Family Allowances Act that was originally introduced, the Youth Allowances Act, and Bill C-264, had one principle in common. Bill C-264, introduced last fall on! September 13 and thrown on March 15 into the ash can of/ desuetude, had about it a different principle, a different^ philosophy, a different legal concept from that now substituted in the present bill. Nowhere has there been an explanation by the minister. At page 1133 of Hansard for March 24 last he said this:

I do not like that abbreviation. Somebody is liable to think the "P" is an "H".
-benefits will provide a basic income for each child upon which can be built additional supports as deemed appropriate by provin-
March 28, 1972

cial or municipal authorities. We know that unemployment insurance does not make any special provision for children. Neither do old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, the Canada Pension Plan retirement pension or war veterans allowances.
He might have added: "Neither does FISP".
Section 5 of the Family Allowances Act as enacted by this parliament provides:
The allowance shall be applied by the person receiving it exclusively toward the maintenance, care, training, education and advancement of the child-
That was the concept that moved Mr. King. Subsection (1) of section 5 of the Youth Allowances Act provides:
An allowance payable to a parent in respect of a dependent youth shall be applied exclusively for the care, maintenance, education or advancement of such youth.
Clause 5 (2) of Bill C-264 introduced last session-see the great change that took place here-provided:
A benefit shall be applied
(a)	in the case of a child referred to in paragraph 3(l)(a), exclusively toward the maintenance, care, training, education or advancement of the child in respect of whom it was paid, and
(b)	in the case of a person referred to in paragraph 3(l)(b), exclusively toward the maintenance, care, training, education or advancement of the person in respect of whom it was paid in such manner as is prescribed by regulations,
Why were the trust provisions for the benefit of the children taken out? Why has this change come about? Those provisions do not appear in the present bill. Instead, this bill takes away the vested right of the children, a right that the minister said

and wrongly said- was the only right they now possess. What does this bill propose to substitute? It proposes outright grants to adults. The children become part of a formula upon which the right of the adult is based and calculated.
I suggest there is something behind this. Negotiations have been going on with the premier of the province of Quebec since the Victoria charter. Did this suggestion come from him? If not, from whom? Clause 5 provides that the recipient of an allowance shall be the parent or other authorized person. The definition of "family" and "parent" refers to the child as being in the custody and control of such person. Again I ask, why was this change brought about? This is a complete abnegation and denial of the basic principles upon which the family allowance legislation and the other legislation, including the bill introduced last September, were founded, and properly so.
One may wonder when this legislation is going to come into effect, whether before or after the election. There is a provision which states it is to come into effect on September 1. I dislike having to take a different view from that expressed by the commentator Mr. Charles Lynch, who has keyhole opportunities to make prophetic utterances. The other day, when the Prime Minister was talking to some youngsters at a collegiate, Mr. Lynch was quite certain the election would take place on October 4. I do not believe that. Some 1,050,000 Canadian families will go off family allowance, so do you think, Mr. Speaker, that this government is going to bring in legislation that is made effective before the election so that those people realize that they are out?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
They are not that stupid.
Family Income Security Plan

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
On the other l and, by getting the legislation through-and I am always one who believes what the government says, to an extent-they will be able to go to two million people and say to them: "Look at the tremendous amount you are going to receive". Less attention will be paid in the Liberal literature to the 1,050,000 Canadians who are going to get nothing than to the tremendous magnificence that will have to wait only for the election result.
In connection with the so-called, misnamed, two price system, the cheques will be going out within the next three weeks, and they will be just like manna from heaven. Therefore, my prediction-and the Prime Minister has not even let his backbenchers or cabinet know when the date is going to be-is that this bill is convincing evidence that the election will not be postponed until fall, despite the fact that I am told that Liberal members from some parts of Canada, even including British Columbia, would like the election in the fall. Those from the province of Quebec would like it earlier, though the Ontario Liberal members would not really like it at all. I am not going to go into particulars of the legislation because, as I say, that has been covered well by the hon. member for Simcoe North and other hon. members who have spoken. I do ask one thing: Why the fixing of the ceiling at an income of $10,000?
Mention was' made by the last hon. gentleman who spoke of the intricacies of the wording of this bill. I have never seen so many words chasing one idea in such a way that nobody knows what the idea is. William Jennings Bryan was one of those who used a multiplicity of words. When somebody said he was going to be defeated in the election, instead of saying do not count your chickens before they are hatched he said, "Do not compute the totality of your poultry population until all of the manifestations of incubation have been entirely completed". That is an example of the way this legislation is worded.
I believe that with the tremendous increase in the cost of living, and the prophesy made the other day by the Governor of the Bank of Canada that we are apparently just starting up the wall of inflation, in a matter of two or three years $10,000 will be a basic level; indeed, it will be approaching the poverty line. I think the amount is entirely inadequate as a ceiling and it should be raised, otherwise many needy people across Canada, on the basis of the expected tremendous cost of inflation, will be denied a fair deal.
What is behind the wording in the bill? I took it on myself to read the correspondence in connection therewith tabled the other day by the Prime Minister. A letter from the Prime Minister was sent to the Premier of Quebec and other premiers. I have not the time to go into lengthy detail, but parts of the letter are worthy of being read. It provides for a new system of family allowances for Quebec and those provinces which accept it. It proposes to bring about tremendous changes in what has been constitutionally feasible up to the present time. Page 7 of the letter reads:

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
Sir:
As you will appreciate, what is contemplated here is a major adjustment in the federal approach to an important income security measure established by parliament more than twenty-five years ago.
This bill, the letter reads, would -introduce a degree of flexibility in relation to provincial conditions that has been hitherto unknown. It would permit provinces that so wished to move toward an integrated system of family allowances within their boundaries, while still maintaining certain general standards for payments to poorer families. I think the plan would meet the basic requirements necessary for the government of Quebec to establish the integrated system of family allowances that it wishes to introduce. I realize that such arrangements would be as temporary as any statute. But if a constitutional guarantee were needed, this could be contemplated as indicated in the next paragraph.
While the immediate federal proposal relates to the family allowance program, the principles involved are clearly capable of extension to other income support programs.
What has happened and why the change in the wording of parts of this bill since last fall? What has taken place that brought about so important a change in such a short period of time? I can only believe it is because Premier Bourassa said he would not have anything to do with the Victoria Charter unless the government capitulated on the subject of family allowances and other social security measures. The government first said it would not do that. Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult to understand why many of the provincial premiers accepted the Victoria Charter. I suggest that the Premier of Quebec was justified in preventing the implementation of that charter, even though he did so on grounds I would not necessarily support.
What would happen under this charter had it come into effect? I ask this because of the statement made today by the Prime Minister in answer to a question relative to the position being taken by the province of Quebec in abolishing the oath of allegiance to the Queen. From now on, apparently anything can be done to the constitution today. It can be emasculated, even castrated as long as whatever is done will bring about votes in the opinion of the Prime Minister of Canada.
Where is the constitution today? I took strong objection to the language bill, not because of its terms but because it represented a constitutional amendment brought in by the back door through a statute of parliament. The government realized it could not secure passage of a constitutional amendment through which would require the agreement of all the provinces of Canada, therefore the language bill was introduced. I have no apology to make for opposing that bill on that ground, and events since have shown that the one argument I advanced, that nobody could challenge it in the courts, was true. The then Minister of Justice, now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said it could be done, but I said it could not. As soon as there was a challenge by the former Mr. Justice Thorson the government of Canada argued that a private person had no status to take action and succeeded in the courts. That constitutional amendment brought in by statute put an end to the British North America Act and its amendment constitutionally for all time to come. Now, we have the fruit of that family tree.
The FLQ and the Parti Quebecois did take strong objection to the oath of allegiance, and joined with the Liberal
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]
government of that province to abolish the constitutional right and the duty that is provided for in the constitution, Section 128 of the British North America Act. This is part of the picture epitomized in this legislation and the changes which have been made in the last few months. This section reads:
Every Member of the Senate or Houses of Commons of Canada shall before taking his Seat therein take and subscribe before the Governor General or some Person authorized by him, and every Member of a Legislative Council or Legislative Assembly of any Province shall before taking his Seat therein take and subscribe before the Lieutenant Governor of the Province or some Person authorized by him, the Oath of Allegiance-
That is the provision in that constitution and it cannot be tinkered with by any province, even though the government of Canada under the present Prime Minister has cut through the constitution as though it did not exist. When I asked him today whether or not this action, which is a complete denial of Section 128 and the whole principle of confederation as embodied in the British North America Act, was wrong and whether he would instruct or advise the Lieutenant Governor of the province of Quebec, the Queen's representative of that province, to withhold royal consent pending consideration by the Governor in Council, he gave an answer of sorts. I cannot describe it, but with that nonchalance which used to be regarded as wisdom contended that disallowance is not being used any more. He claimed that it is as dead as the right of veto of the Imperial Parliament over the Parliament of Canada. Is it?
In respect of the Lieutenant-Governor's discretionary powers and the executive process of the Crown I will read from the comments of J. R. Mallory. The government of Canada asked the Lieutenant-Governor of the province of Alberta to withhold Royal Assent to legislation such as the Bank Act and other things of the time. Mr. Mallory summarizes as follows:
The revival of the power in Alberta in 1937 caused general surprise. It had become widely believed that the power had become constitutionally obsolete in the same way that the position of the governor general as an imperial officer had disappeared as a result of the achievement of Canadian autonomy. So general was the uncertainty that the federal government referred the whole question of the scope and validity of the powers of disallowance, reservation, and withholding assent to the Supreme Court in the autumn of 1937.
The Supreme Court had no difficulty in finding that these powers continued to subsist, unaffected by changes in constitutional conventions, and the powers were equally valid, whether the legislation was intra vires the provincial legislature or not, and that the only limitations on the discretion of the lieutenant-governor were instructions from the governor general.
Now, we see the present constitutional picture being unveiled. Today is a dark day in the history of Canada's constitution when the Prime Minister, the Queen's first minister, says we will let the provinces do whatever they want to do whether or not it is constitutional and will not ask for reservation being made because to do so is obsolete. The Victoria Charter was turned down as a result of Premier Bourassa's opposition. I am glad he did so. His objection to that charter is proved in the present change in the bill as introduced last September.
March 28, 1972

The Victoria Charter would have hamstrung Canada's future for generations to come. The Bill of Rights would have been reduced to virtual innocuity. The Supreme Court of Canada would have been a body in which judges would be expected to decide cases on the basis of geographical location rather than on the law. There would be no chance for the provinces of Manitoba or Saskatchewan to ever have anything to do with the amendments because they would have to have 50 per cent of the population of the four western provinces in order to have the right to object to or advance constitutional amendments. We will never, in those provinces, have 50 per cent of the population with the populations of Alberta and British Columbia increasing as they are. This is what is happening to our constitution. Finally the protection of the English language under the British North America Act would have been removed. This legislation shows a fine Machiavellian hand. I shall not say an Italian hand. We have the answer given by the Prime Minister of Canada today that this government does not intend to do anything about it and that from now on the provinces of Canada will be free to make any changes they desire in the constitution. This day represents one that will be looked back on in the years ahead as the natural culmination of a disunited Canada with the monarchy being undermined. The constitution will not be in existence. Every Father of Confederation, including the French Canadian representative, recommended or demanded the preservation of the monarchy.
The second fruit of the family tree is the changes in this bill. In order to obtain this agreement in respect of the Victoria Charter which I say would destroy the hope of one Canada, one nation, the erosion of this constitution is continued with the approval of the Prime Minister. This legislation is introduced in order to provide an excuse to secure the support of a province which took a firm, honourable and reasonable stand. Over the years I have been here I have never known the constitution to be trampled on in the way in which it is being trampled on today. Shades of Mackenzie King and St. Laurent! Where do we go?
Mr. Steven Otto (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services: Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to listen to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). The thrust of his speech ws very impressive. However, as the right hon. gentleman spoke, I wondered whether that part of the constitution was so important that it must override the benefits which are to be provided for children. Do we deny benefits to children in order to preserve a constitution which is changing? The right hon. member knows it is changing. To sit here and say that the constitution will never change just does not make any sense because of the changing relationships with the provinces. The provinces are assuming certain jurisdictions with the federal government just as the federal government is also assuming certain provincial jurisdictions. I think this House should accept that fact. The right hon. gentleman nods his head. He knows I agree with him on the value of a constitution but it must be a new one. There is no sense in putting up our back and saying we will keep it the way it is, because there will have to be a new one.
Family Income Security Plan
What we want is a constitution which is relevant to our times. If I correctly understand some of the speeches made on this bill, I believe the opposition is really based on the fact that the universality of the old law disappears in the selectivity that this bill now brings about. I could be more cautious politically at this time, if indeed we are to have an election, and say that everyone will get their little benefit. However, I believe we should be honest. I am the first to agree that some people will lose the benefits, while others will get more. The right hon. gentlemen from Prince Albert mentioned the preamble in the 1944 bill to the effect that family allowances were meant to assist in the education, the clothing and the welfare of children. In 1944, our economy had not yet reached a stage which would give us perfect security in growth. We anticipated a large increase in the population of children. We knew what the situation was. The Liberal government then introduced a measure which would be of assistance to children. It was assumed that the money received by the mother would be laid on the table in the form of food, or else used to provide clothing. Education was also an important factor because the cost of education was going up, and after the depression not everybody had the necessary money.
Let us look at the position today. How many mothers think that this is money for the children? How many of them think it is a reward to them for having borne children, pin money that they don't have to get from their husbands? We have had a change in emphasis. Now, we provide substantial aid for education, at the federal, provincial and municipal level. We also have provided assistance for housing and many people no longer have to worry about housing. We have welfare plans and widows' allowances. All of these things have been substituted for the dread, the panic and the anxiety that was with us in 1944.
Hon. members opposite say we should continue the scheme. I ask continue what? Should we continue taking money out of one pocket of the taxpayer, and putting it back in another pocket, charging him a few pennies for administrative costs in between? We said we were going to be a reform party, a reform government. We said we would make changes. The real change here is that universality will no longer apply. We have to give more to those people who are in need, and we must discontinue paying those who are really not in need.
From the evidence that I have gathered over the past four or five years, I know that in the lower income bracket the family allowance is used as part of the general household budget. In the higher income brackets it may be used to build an education fund for the children, but the majority of mothers in this group tend to consider it as their own, as largesse from the government to use for their own purposes, for hairdo's and all sorts of things. The government is not some kind of deity that gives out money. This money comes from the taxpayers' own pockets. If we increased the amount of family allowances under the old scheme, the taxpayers would have to pay out more money. Again, Mr. Speaker, the taxpayer is beginning to resist the constant and increasing drain on his pocketbook.

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
It is not true to say that this bill will not hurt some people. But I do not mind telling people in the higher income brackets that they will not continue to get family allowances. Increasing the tax burden by taking money out of one pocket and putting it back into another just does not make sense, and that would be the only alternative.
For the NDP to regret the disappearance of universality is a reversal of their former stand. I point out that it was not the present government that wanted this change. Since 1963 and 1964 there has been a constant demand in the press. At meetings everywhere people were saying that we had to change the family allowance scheme. We are changing it now, Mr. Speaker. But a law cannot be changed in a way that will affect only somebody else. A lot of people over the $10,000 salary level will be affected. I have no qualms at all about saying that I am proud of this bill. It is something that had to come.
Those people who say we don't dare bring this measure forward because an election is coming are advocating a return to the old Tammany Hall style politics, when politicians always warned, "Don't do anything before an election. Keep nice and quiet. After the election is over, then you can throw the book at the people." I think people now want to know what the situation is, and what it will be. Despite my great respect for the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, I do not think that the date this legislation comes into force has had, or will have, any bearing on the Prime Minister's decision to call an election. I do not think he is that kind of Prime Minister. As a matter of fact, the people of Canada know he is not that kind of politician.

I think what irritates members opposite now, especially those people who have been members for a long time, is the fact that I tend to call them old-time politicians. This applies not only to those on the other side, but to those on this side as well.
But, Mr. Speaker, I have found that the new Canadian, the present-day Canadian is more educated, more sophisticated. He wants to be told exactly what you are going to do. He wants to discuss it. Of course, he may complain. Any number of people will complain. Nobody likes change thrown at them all of a sudden. But on reflection, people will admit today that this bill is the only way to deal with this matter. By and large most Canadians will agree that universality no longer applies to such programs as old age pensions, supplementary allowances, family allowances or youth allowances. They know that to continue universality makes no sense. I think that today they will accept the idea of selectivity. They will accept the fact that there are children in Canada who do need more help.
If they, themselves, can do without this help they are pleased that they have the means, that they have the security, to do without it. Despite all the surface complaints, I have a deep conviction that Canadians will not object to this measure. I have confidence in them. I believe that when they see the courage of the government in putting this bill forward, they will not take away their
(Mr. Otto.]
support but show their own confidence in honesty and truth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak at this particular stage in the debate and to follow the hon. member who has just spoken. I have to disagree with just about everything he said. I cannot think of a more opportune moment to enter a debate such as this, because what the hon. member is endeavouring to say in a philosophical way is that the government can continue to tax the middle income group to an ever-increasing degree and anticipate that they are going to produce the revenues needed to look after everybody else in the nation. In other words, the harder you work and the more you earn, the greater the degree of discrimination practised against you by this government. If the hon. member thinks that people will continue to put up with this sort of government philosophy he is in for a shock when the election comes, whether it be this spring, this summer, this fall or next year.
I think it is a crying shame that the principle of universality in the family allowance measure is being destroyed. I think it is a crying shame that once again the middle income group has found that the government's legislation, as was the case with the so-called tax reform measure, is going to discriminate against them and make them pay the fiddler without allowing them to dance. I think the time has come in this parliament when members should speak out and try to stop those people who are making this country what it is today. If we are moving ahead, if things are getting better, by and large it is the result of the efforts of the people who are discriminated against by this sort of legislation.
Unfortunately, for too long these people have felt that the government is like a bloodsucker, a real leech. Every time it is looking for funds for the various programs that it feels may have some political value, it lands on them and draws more blood. What this government does not appear to realize is that it also draws more incentive out of these people. The more it draws out, the less is left in the nation and, basically, this is the reason we have over 600,000 unemployed in this country. People are getting sick and tired of working so that they can turn over most of their earnings to the government to help out those who, for one reason or another, are not able to look after themselves.
I believe we have gone well beyond the limit in taxing the middle income group. I believe we are destroying the incentive of this nation by this type of legislation, and I believe the end to this type of philosophy had better come in a big hurry or we will find ourselves in an even worse mess than we are today. God knows, it is difficult to imagine how we could be in a worse mess.

Mr. Speaker, the other thing that bothers me a lot is that once again the government of Canada is involving itself in a form of means test. There is a philosophy in Canada that abhors the means test or the needs test or whatever you want to call it because it is distaste-
March 28, 1972

ful. We can go back to the 1930's if we so desire-and this government has taken us there in many ways, certainly as far as unemployment is concerned. We can recall how the dignity of the individual was destroyed when there was no work and he was subjected to the investigative procedures of municipal, provincial and federal governments in order to get enough bread on his table for his family.
This type of legislation is taking us back to that philosophy. When the Canada Assistance Plan was before the House I spoke up because it embodied the same type of philosophy, the investigation of the individual to determine whether he should get what he requires to keep himself alive. Once that principle is adopted, there is a proliferation of bureaucracy. In the end, as you destroy universality by saying there are some people receiving benefits who do not require them without adding the rider that they are entitled to them because the tax they pay gives them that right, you do two other things. First of all you destroy a person's dignity and, secondly, you take away his liberty. Every time a bureaucrat walks into a home and wants to know this and that, the individual has lost certain inalienable rights. I oppose this, Mr. Speaker, as strongly as I can but this is what is happening in Canada over and over again as a result of legislation of the type proposed.
In a couple of years after this plan comes into effect, after we have eliminated over a million people from the family allowance rolls, after we do all that and make an assessment of how much it costs, we will probably discover that it is costing more to be selective than it would have cost to give it to everybody.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: That is true of welfare right now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) says this is true of welfare right now, and I agree with him. This is the most damnable thing about this type of legislation, the minute you bring in selectivity and eliminate universality you interfere with the rights of people and bring in bureaucrats by the hundreds of thousands who go around investigating people and building up files to which other people may have access. These people are subjected to all kinds of investigative procedures which are very destructive.
The hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) says you delay the procedure and that is correct. You delay people from securing immediately what they have a right to while bureaucrats determine whether they should approve or disapprove. Members of parliament will not vote against family allowances, even though under this bill the government will wipe out family allowances for over one million people. They will not vote against the bill because through it the government will provide greater benefits for many millions of people. No member of parliament wants to prevent people securing additional benefits at a time when living costs seem to be almost out of control. However, Mr. Speaker, that should not prevent a member of parliament from saying that the legislation before the House should be much better than that being proposed by the government.
Family Income Security Flan
I say, Sir, that since November 30 we have been considering some type of family income security plan. Despite all the time spent in thinking about the legislation, Canadians in general will be given legislation that is less beneficial than that presently existing. A great many Canadians will get nothing except an additional bill to pay. When asked to pay the bill they will be told that they are not to derive any benefits from their additional payments. This situation is something like the one involving the postal service of Canada. It costs twice as much to send a letter that will take twice as long getting to its destination, as compared with previous days. Producing that kind of legislation for the people of Canada seems to be almost inbred in this government's approach to legislative priorities.
So far as I am concerned, this particular piece of legislation will not have any significant anti-poverty effect in this nation. Even in the Atlantic region, which probably will benefit to a greater extent than any other part of Canada, the impact of this legislation on poverty will not be all that significant. The number of people who face poverty the day before the new payments are sent out will not be substantially different from the number who face poverty the day after the new cheques are sent out. What would help us would be legislation that would produce jobs. This is the subject we ought to be debating. At present, even though we are debating the bill before us, we do not know when the new cheques are to be sent out.
Last September constituents of mine telephoned me to ask why their family allowance cheques were the same as before. In July or August, the government had announced that new family allowances at higher rates would be available in September. I had to tell those people that, according to what I had learned in the House of Commons, the September date had been changed to May 1, 1972. Now I must tell those same people that instead of being implemented in May, this bill is to be implemented some day but I do not know when. The government is not telling me, and it is not telling them. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough, and the people of Canada will not think it is good enough. If the hon. member who spoke just before I entered this debate thinks that is good enough, that is just dandy. His attitude is probably a very good indication that he will be replaced in the next general election, whenever that comes.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) was right in suggesting that for the Liberal members representing Ontario constituencies there is no satisfactory date for a general election. Neither 1972 nor 1973 is satisfactory so far as those Liberal members of parliament are concerned. If the philosophy of the hon. member who spoke just before I did is an example of the philosophy of federal Liberal members representing Ontario constituencies, they are in trouble. Any day will be a bad day, so far as they are concerned, for a general election, no matter whether it comes in spring, summer or fall.
When we return after the Easter recess, I hope the government will introduce legislation that will help all families which are to receive family allowances as well as families which need help through forms of income security that do not involve any package being considered by

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) or any other minister of this government. I hope such legislation will produce employment for the more than 600,000 people who find themselves without work and want to work. I do not know how much longer this government can expect the people of this country to put up with its relaxed and nonchalant approach to the serious problem of poverty facing so many in this nation.
I repeat, the middle income earner of this country has been the goat for far too long. It is time we put a stop to legislation of the type now before the House. Under it, the middle income earner is to be penalized, because he is industrious and trying to make a contribution to building a better Canada. He is making his contribution and assisting his fellow man by working and earning. We must put a stop to legislation of this kind. Every middle income earner in this country has as much right to family allowances, if he has children, as any other person in Canada. Unfortunately for him, because of the government's philosophy, he has been cut off at the pass. He is being made to foot the bill, and he will receive no benefits. He has been asked to do this time and again. I am fed up with this treatment, and I am sure he is; I am sure the government will discover just how fed up he is when it calls the election.

At the same time, out of the other side of his mouth he speaks about the poverty situation in Canada, the poor and how this government is lackadaisical about doing anything for the poor. I cannot put the two statements together so that they make any kind of sense.

speechtext: That is the problem with you fellows over there.

speechtext:
It may be, but you do not have the answer, either. You are talking about the abominable tax on the middle income group. I agree that the middle income group in Canada may be carrying more than its share of the tax. However, that system has been accepted as the proper system in Canada for decades. The aim of that system has been to improve the lot of the poor people by moving them into the middle income group. Where are we to get the money to help the poor? Is it the proposition of the Conservative party that we should tax the corporations to a greater degree? I thought the proposition of that party was to allow the corporations free-wheeling rights so they could invest their profits and create jobs rather than take more tax from them. I thought their proposition was that taxes should be reduced in that area.
What should we do? Should we tax the poor to a higher degree? The money that is paid out in the form of family allowances or family income security, and the people of

Canada know this, does not grow on trees. It comes out of the pockets of the taxpayers. What group forms the biggest tax-paying base in Canada? It happens to be the middle income group. I am glad to subscribe to the philosophy enunciated by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). He said that the people in this group are prepared to face up to their responsibilities and do something for the less fortunate in the country. They are not acting like dogs in a manger by saying "I've got mine; now, Charlie, you try to get yours". They are prepared to take part in this exercise. I am prepared to accept his philosophy in that regard.
The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North deplored the loss of universality. I agree that in many ways universality is a fine concept. However, as a member of parliament, assuming I only have one child and that I draw a salary of $18,000 a year, I find it difficult to understand why I should get a cheque in the same amount as a working man with one child who only earns $4,000 a year. I do not buy that. The time for universality in Canada has ended.
Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) mentioned that universality worked because you put money into the hands of all individuals and then get it back from those who do not meet it through taxes. This system works in the case of old age pensions where $75 or $80 a month is paid out, is counted as income and those in the higher income groups repay most or all of it to the government in taxes. I remind hon. members that that principle does not apply to family allowances. The money goes into the family, but it is not counted as income. Therefore, the principle of universality does not work in the same way when applied to family income security, baby bonus or whatever you want to call it, as it does when applied to old age pensions. The time for universality, in the sense that it was being used for purposes of family allowances, is gone.
There are many poor people in Canada who need additional assistance. The pie is just so big. It should be distributed among the people who are hungry, not among those who are well off. The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North referred to the government as a bloodsucker sucking funds from the middle class group for its own benefit. I suggest the hon. member does not have the respect that I do for the intelligence of the voters of Canada. The voters of Canada know that the government is not coining money in the Mint or printing it in the basement and handing it out to people. They know that the money that is paid out to various groups in Canada comes from the people of Canada.
To suggest that this government would think that by increasing family allowances to a certain number of the population would result in an increase in its popularity is an insult to the intelligence of the voters of Canada. However, I believe the hon. member indicated that. While he deplored the fact that the government was proceeding in this way, he spoke vociferously about the business of ridding ourselves of the concept of universality and criticized as strongly as he could what he called the re-introduction of the means test. In his next breath, he said "but I won't vote against it". Why will he not vote against it? The reason is that a number of people in Canada, particu-
March 28, 1972

larly in the hon. member's constituency, are going to receive increased benefits as a result of this change. He would not want to deprive them of those increased benefits. despite the fact this measure goes against his highest principles, because those people have a vote in the next election.
The hon. member deplored the introduction of some kind of means test, and mentioned how the introduction of this method of distributing money would result in a proliferation of bureaucrats. To quote him, one result would be the employment of bureaucrats by the hundreds of thousands. As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, the distribution of these new family allowances is based on income tax returns which are already being made by all of the taxpaying citizens of Canada. It is on the basis of those returns that this family income security money will be distributed. There is no question about the introduction of additional hundreds of thousands of bureaucrats. I suggest that, like many of his colleagues, he is thinking of 30 or 40 years ago, when the means test was a mean and miserable way of dealing out dole as it were.
I heard some of the examples cited yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). I agree with her wholeheartedly. When we reached the stage at which parents, to prove their children were unable to support them, had to bring the children into court in order to qualify for assistance, I agree wholeheartedly with the hon. lady that we had got ourselves into a deplorable position. Surely, though, the plan we are talking about today is not that type of plan. It is a plan geared to returns which are already being made by taxpayers. It no longer implies a demeaning inquisition by government bureaucrats or the services of the numbers of government bureaucrats who were involved in the system in the late twenties and thirties. Fortunately, the present government, and governments before it in Canada, have recognized the folly of their ways. They have made changes and brought the system up to date to the point at which it is now a reasonable and practical proposition on the basis of which we can make the best possible use of the resources available to us.
One of the hon. members opposite who spoke this afternoon said: Retain the universality principle but raise the allowances for everybody. I agree with him in a sense. That would be absolutely great, provided we had the money. I should like to drive a Cadillac. I can only afford to drive a Volkswagen. I wish the hon. member would keep this in mind when dealing with the facts of the situation in Canada-the amount of funds and resources available to 22 million Canadians to take care of the poor and the elderly. Let us keep an eye, after all, on the resources which are available to us.
I cannot end without commenting on the speech made by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), for whom I have the highest respect. I must say I only heard the latter part of his remarks, that dealing with the constitution. The right hon. member has a great appreciation of the constitution which was written ifl>1867. So has everyone. But today is 1972. Canada is not the same today as it was in 1867 and a constitution written in 1867 is not necessarily the best constitution for Canada in
Family Income Security Plan
1972. I gather from the right hon. gentleman's comments that change is alien to his nature. I hope he will reconsider and realize that constitutional change is an absolute necessity if we are to continue as one united Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to a number of speeches this afternoon. They were not at all similar, but in my opinion they were well made. I was particularly interested to hear the last speaker refer to the desirability of establishing uniform legislation which would take into account the situations of those who are poor and those who are rich and distribute wealth on a selected basis providing more for those at the low end than for those at the high end. I wonder why the hon. member has not sat down with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), who is involved in many pieces of legislation concerned with establishing minimum incomes, in an attempt to arrive at some way of arranging for a guaranteed annual income so that we might move away from what the hon. member obviously acknowledges to be the deficiencies of the legislation before us.
I am prepared to put on record the difficulties arising from the relationship between family allowances as contemplated in Bill C-170 and the income tax structure set out in Bill C-169. We reach a position under that tax structure which would allow a fairly large payment at the low end of the income scale, but also a very large deduction from tax at the other end. In effect, this is really making provision of a high amount for children at the low end, through family allowances, and at the top as a substantial deduction in respect of children whose parents enjoy very high incomes-I am talking about income as high as $100,000 a year.
One of the objections to the proposition before us is that we are abandoning what we really set out to achieve in the beginning, that is to say, the provision of something special for the children regardless of their parents ability to earn.
It has been said that the middle class is paying the shot-that the middle class does not need this money. This is not really my experience. I believe we are now confronted with a totally new poverty level in Canada, and this poverty level is not necessarily below $10,000. For instance, I know many teachers who are earning between $10,000 and $14,000 and who are not getting enough money to meet their needs. This is because their standard of living has increased considerably and they are finding great difficulty in maintaining this level. Now, when these people are experiencing great financial difficulty, exactly the same thing happens with respect to children in those families as to any other children. The two cars in the garage cost so much a month to maintain. The $40,000 house costs so much to maintain. There are bills for heating, medical expenses and so on. There is only a certain amount of money to be spent on these things, and if it is not enough, what happens? There is a shortage of food and the children are eating hamburgers. So we are not going far enough if we simply take a certain level and say it is a reasonable level of income.
I read a story the other day in a Toronto newspaper which maintained that a family consisting of parents and two children, who own their own house and car, were

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
living at poverty level although the family earnings amounted to $11,000. The two children were attending university. I suppose it depends entirely on the way in which a family distributes its income, or on the type of society in which we live. Members of parliament are familiar with this situation. Since I have been here our wages have been increased on three occasions. I find that no matter how high my wages are I can find some way of spending them all. There is always some way of distributing the money. I suppose this is true of everyone in every category.
I heard of a case the other day involving a family which was very worried about two things. These people live in a house which is worth, I suppose, about $300. Their income, I presume, would be less than $1,000 a year. I am quite sure they were not receiving welfare or any kind of assistance at all. Two of the children go to high school. The mother says: "I don't know what my daughters do with their stockings." I continually have to buy nylon stockings. She also pointed out that she was obliged to pay $4 to buy a book. The sum of $4 is an immense amount of money for that family, but they were willing to pay it. I imagine the reason they were willing to pay it was that they got the money in the form of a family allowance, as a right, and it was used for the purpose for which it was intended.
In many cases this is also true in families of higher income. For example, take the family that drinks too much, or which has drug problems or monetary problems. The fact that there is a large income coming into the house does not necessarily mean that the children get any of the benefits. They may, or they may not. But in many cases a universal payment given to them as children as a right has been of exceeding advantage to those children.
I am of the opinion that one of the reasons the government is now moving away from universality is that it is considering a guaranteed income for Canadians. If that is so, then I am fully in support of it. But if it is so, then let the government be brave and introduce such a proposal now instead of playing around with it. If we pass this piece of legislation as it is, no one, but no one, will know how it operates. Let me just read one small paragraph and ask the minister for a quick explanation of it. This is a complete sentence:
Where at any time during the first eleven months of a benefit year, other than the fourth month, or during the eight-month period next before that benefit year a parent-
And so on it goes. Another example:
(b) where the parents of the child were not resident in Canada for the complete base calendar year, unless a statement of the estimated income of the child's family for the first calendar year thereafter in which the parents reasonably expect to be resident in Canada has been submitted by the parents, in which case the income of the child's family for that calendar year shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
There are many clauses of the bill like that which do not make sense. I would advise the minister to look at them closely, because he is doing in this bill exactly what we did with the unemployment insurance legislation

putting in an "and" or a "this" or a "that", and giving alternatives.

As far as the unemployment insurance legislation is concerned, by doing this we literally created chaos. The calculations that will have to be made in this legislation will require use of a computer. First of all, you will have to compute your income for the previous year, or people will have the alternative of establishing a base year, whether the previous year or a projected base year, at one's discretion. This information will be fed into the computer along with other facts and figures, such as age of the child, number of children in the family and so on. Each will be separately calculated. Then, during the year you will have to decide, either at the end of the fourth month or the eighth month period before the end of the benefit year, whether you ceased to be employed, and so on. You will be faced with many choices for the computer.
This will mean the minister will have to engage the services of inspectors. Just to give the House an example of what this means, an inspector for the Unemployment Insurance Commission visited a man in my area the other day. The man was not home, but the reason the inspector called was that this man had reported some part time earnings the previous week and the inspector was checking whether he was making more money than he claimed. The inspector telephoned this man's wife at her work and asked where her husband was. She replied he was in southern Ontario. He asked for his telephone number, but his wife replied that he was looking for work and that he telephoned her every night. The inspector reported this man was unavailable for work since they were unable to telephone him.
This is the kind of inspector who will be appointed under this act. These inspectors will have to find out what money people made previously. There will be inspectors to find out what people are making now. If a wife works for two months, this will alter the annual budget information that is fed into the computer and the information will have to be refed to the computer. If the wife receives unemployment insurance benefits, she will have to calculate the wage that she has received which is added to family income. Thousands of calculations will have to be made during the lifetime of a family. In other words, bureaucracy will grow to an immense size.
I see nothing wrong in this country with establishing an income tax structure which will absorb any payment made universally for which there is no need. One would know at the end of the year whether or not one had received too much money. If one had, this amount could be paid back through the income tax structure. If not, the money is kept by the recipient. I fully realize we have been through the Income Tax Act a number of times. I understand that one major company hired six or seven lawyers and sent them away to a quiet area to study the recent act. Having looked at it, they came back and said they could not come to any conclusions which they felt would be helpful to the company because they really did not understand what the act was all about. I sympathize with them because I think that is true of nearly everybody. I think there will be much cause for amusement in this country, in addition to television, when people try to complete their income tax forms for the first time under the new act in 1973. I suppose it will be the national pastime for several months.
