subsubtopic: MEASURE RESTRICTING USE OF THESE DESCRIPTIVE WORDS
speechtext:
that Bill C-78, respecting the use of the expression "Parliament Hill", be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps at the outset I should thank hon. members for agreeing to have this bill brought forward for consideration today. I appreciate that courtesy and I want hon. members to know that I do.
The bill itself is quite simple. It is an attempt to prevent the commercial use of the words "Parliament Hill" to designate any property or place, or to identify any articles for sale or to otherwise identify any commercial enterprise for commercial use. It is very simple in its form and I think it is clear from its language.
The reason for the bill is the usage of the term "Parliament Hill" to designate a very fine new hotel in Ottawa. I might add that it is a much needed and very good new hotel. In November of last year the hotel, in a large advertisement in one of the Ottawa newspapers, indicated that the hotel was on Parliament Hill, which it is not, and the intention to use the designation "Parliament Hill" to identify that hotel as one of a number of hotels in a chain. This error was immediately drawn to the attention of the hotel and I thought the matter had then been concluded. In February of this year it became clear, when the hotel was about to open, that the name had not been changed. This matter was again drawn to their attention and notice of this bill was filed at that time. The hotel immediately took steps within its organization to change the designation of that hotel to a more appropriate one. I want to acknowledge and thank the hotel for its courtesy and action, or its maturity, however one wishes to express it. In any event I want to express appreciation for their action when the matter was brought to their attention.
As best I can ascertain, there has been no attempt to use this designation by any other enterprise in the first 102 years of confederation. Last year a farm near Ottawa chose this designation and applied it to certain livestock records in respect of cattle. There is also a small sports clothing or sports goods shop which has started to use the name. These are very recent cases and so far as I know there are no others. It seems to me this is a most inappropriate designation as applied to anything other than this immediate area and grounds on which the Parliament Buildings are situated, and the name should be reserved for that purpose.

I tried to make the bill very simple, providing that the words "Parliament Hill" should not be used for the three purposes set out in Clause 1 (a), (b), (c), that is to designate a property or location, to identify any goods, merchandise, wares or articles for commercial use or sale, or in association with a commercial service rendering establishment.
There is in addition a simple provision that a breach of these provisions is an offence punishable on summary conviction. Then, there is a clause which makes it clear that the bill in no way limits or interferes with the powers, privileges, rights and immunities of both Houses of Parliament and their members. That provision was put in because there had been some academic discussion concerning whether the use of the term would in fact constitute technically a breach of the privileges of parliament. That is not an argument or a reason which I assert for bringing forward this bill. However, that argument has been made and I thought it wise and appropriate to include a provision in the bill making it clear that the bill in no way limits the powers, privileges, rights and immunities of both Houses of Parliament and their members.
There is one other matter I should draw to the attention of hon. gentlemen. If it is agreeable to the House I should like to ask permission to change the wording of the motion so that instead of providing that the bill be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, it read that the bill be read a second time and referred to the committee of the whole. Then, we could proceed today to the committee of the whole stage and third reading if that is agreeable to hon. members.

As to the second point raised about other buildings being used to house members of parliament in the course of their duties, and the example given of the Confederation Building, which is outside the area described in the bill, I did give this a good deal of attention and thought. It appeared to me that it was better to refer in this legislation at this time to the area clearly and commonly defined as Parliament Hill. If and when arrangements are made to house members of parliament in an area off Parliament Hill, there will be other questions to be settled affecting their privileges, so that the privileges they have, and have always had traditionally, will be clearly protected at that stage. Then, the definition of the area may have to be changed when dealing with those other matters. I came to the conclusion that it was best not to try to anticipate any such change, and contented myself with a description that was soundly based, that should have support in law, and the support of hon. members as a reasonable approach.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY FROM DEFINITION OF EARNINGS
speechtext:
that Bill C-180, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 (holiday pay), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity, through the generous consideration of the House and my seatmate the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), to speak on this bill. Its purpose is very simple and I hope it will be treated in the same way as the other bills we have considered in this hour. I hope we can deal with the bill in committee this afternoon and make progress toward its passage. As hon. members know, the question of holiday pay is under the jurisdiction of provincial governments. Most governments that have passed legislation on vacation pay have deducted at least 2 per cent of a worker's earnings and set this amount aside for his regular annual holiday.
In the province of Ontario, where I am familiar with the operation of the vacation pay act, the purpose was that a person could take one week's holiday and receive for that period the amount which he would normally earn. The desire to implement holiday pay in Ontario stemmed both from the advantages that flow to the employee, which were fairly obvious, and to the employer. It was the feeling that if the employee were to get one week's holiday with pay in the summer he would be apt to produce more efficiently when he returned to work. Most unions have negotiated an additional week's holiday and there are in some cases arrangements which provide for up to five weeks' holiday after 20 years of service.
One of the things the Ontario government did in their legislation was to ensure that vacation pay was not available to an employee until July 2. This was because we live in the northern hemisphere and have a relatively short period of sunshine. In the mines and in the factories we have not been able to provide the kind of lighting that would give enough vitamin C, so it was thought that if the worker took vacation pay after July 2 he could take his family to the beach or elsewhere to get the sun. Obviously, if he could take the vacation pay at a time of his own choosing, he might take it when he needs extra money. It was therefore decided that it would not be available to him until July 2.
Other benefits have been negotiated by unions over the years. One that has become very important in the last ten years is severance pay. This is negotiated by unions with companies against the day when the company will no longer be able to employ as many workers, particularly in fields where technological change is a real possibility and retraining will be necessary. There has been set aside a sum of money which can be used by the employee in addition to other moneys that he might have in order to make the transition between jobs. This government has agreed that in some cases where a worker has to move from one area to another it will make enough money available to the Department of Manpower and Immigra-
March 28, 1972

tion to move the family and furniture to the new location. However, everyone who has moved his home knows that while this may cover the actual moving cost it does not cover the upheaval that takes place when a person travels from one area to another to find a job.
As our technology improves and specialization in industry involves more and more retraining of workers, severance pay becomes a very important part of the protection provided to the worker. When the Unemployment Insurance Commission began calculating benefits they took into consideration a number of items they called "other moneys". These include, of course, insurance against loss of wages which one can take out, training allowances and "other moneys" which their handbook defines as follows:
Other moneys: You must declare all moneys you have received or will receive for the period for which you are reporting, even if you did not work. This includes vacation pay, temporary workmen's compensation payments, bonuses, gratuities, severance pay, etc. Be sure to give a brief explanation of the moneys received in the space provided on your report form.
Mr. Speaker, it is my hope that other hon. members will agree that there were many reasons for establishing benefits such as vacation pay, severance pay and workmen's compensation, and that these should not be included as moneys earned by an employee while unemployed. It is for this reason I have introduced this bill and I strongly urge those members who believe in severance pay and vacation pay to support it.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY FROM DEFINITION OF EARNINGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the measure before us this afternoon concerning vacation with pay has caused a degree of unhappiness to people who become unemployed, particularly those engaged in seasonal work, who have seen legislation introduced that did not exist under the old Unemployment Insurance Act.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY FROM DEFINITION OF EARNINGS
speechtext: That is putting it very mildly.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY FROM DEFINITION OF EARNINGS
speechtext:
It is a regulation that was introduced in the new act and to some extent it has detracted from the general quality of the Unemployment Insurance Act passed last summer by this parliament. Another effect of this regulation, Mr. Speaker, is that it has caused an anomaly which works in favour of those who become unemployed and who are members of a union or an organization which has agreed with the employer upon a system of so-called vacation with pay to be payable at a certain date.
As a result of this vacation with pay fund agreed upon with the employer, it is possible for people who become unemployed and nave the benefit of this arrangement to withdraw money from the fund as payment for vacation only on a date specified usually in the agreement with the union. If you become unemployed at any other time of year you will not receive this vacation with pay sum and, therefore, since the money is not available it is not calculated against your claim and is not deducted from the benefits you hope to receive.
As a result, people who become unemployed and fall into the category I have mentioned enjoy a benefit that is usually not enjoyed by the vast majority of workers who become unemployed and do not belong to a union that has
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
negotiated such an arrangement with the employer. Therefore, there is dual treatment of unemployed people. Those who have entered into this kind of arrangement with the employer can look forward to a higher level of payment for a greater number of weeks, whereas for those who do not enjoy the benefit of this arrangement their vacation with pay moneys are included in the calculation of unemployment insurance entitlement. Thus, they pay the consequence of not having been able to organize themselves as well as other workers and for not being able to work out with their employers a vacation with pay agreement that others have entered into.
This situation, Mr. Speaker, was brought to the minister's attention several months ago and has caused considerable unhappiness particularly in the construction industry where the level of employment fluctuates from season to season. Of course, when workers are thrown out of work or become unemployed and are not covered by a specific vacation with pay agreement with the employer, their vacation with pay entitlement becomes part and parcel of the total calculation respecting unemployment insurance benefits.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) also made the point that the vacation with pay payment to a great extent represents 2 per cent of the salary that a man has earned and saved while employed, and it stands to reason that this form of saving ought to be made available to the man when he becomes unemployed. It should not be deducted from the payment he looks forward to receiving under unemployment insurance.
These two matters, Mr. Speaker, have probably been brought forward for consideration because the new approach to this question is one based on cessation of income. So long as we call the present scheme unemployment insurance it will be considered by the men concerned as a form of insurance payable when they become unemployed. If vacation with pay benefits are due to people as a result of their work and earnings, those payments represent an additional resource on which they can count in time of need to meet expenses which may be unpredictable. The vacation with pay payment should not be confused with entitlement to unemployment insurance.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY FROM DEFINITION OF EARNINGS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT. 1971 AMENDMENT TO EXCLUDE HOLIDAY AND SEVERANCE PAY FROM DEFINITION OF EARNINGS

In this sense, the hon. member for Timiskaming has rendered a great service to a vast number of people across the nation who are now struggling, as they have been for the past few months, with unemployment insurance regulations. They have suffered as a result of a calculation which it is felt, and rightly so, should not have been made.
It is distressing to see what has happened to a piece of legislation passed by parliament. In the practical application of that legislation, in day to day dealings with people affected one finds that the concept in the minds of the legislators who originally approved this very fine piece of legislation has been greatly distorted. Parliament intended to increase benefits and to make them available to people who had contributed to the fund for a shorter period than previously was necessary. At the same time, parliament wanted our people to enjoy a standard of living that would not be reduced to the level where a man

March 28, 1972
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
would need to be truly concerned as to whether he could meet his day to day commitments for the upkeep of his household and the maintenance of his family. Vacation with pay is the type of extra that in this day and age, when living costs are increasing, is essential if a family is to survive the tragedy of sudden unemployment.
I do not share the view expressed a few moments ago by the hon, member for Timiskaming that perhaps a man would need this payment in order to move to a job in another region. Such costs are supposed to be taken care of by the manpower mobility program. Certainly, vacation with pay payments will be utilized by the people affected in a manner that is not extravagant. Such payments will help to meet the basic, substantial needs of a breadwinner who suddenly, for reasons beyond his control, loses his job.
It seemed to me, therefore, that I ought to take this opportunity to speak in support of this measure and express the thoughts expressed to me over the last few months by a number of people. People are dissatisfied with the measure which was introduced by means of regulation and which is causing hardship that is unwarranted. Such regulations need to be removed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before private members' hour I was drawing attention to the difficulties which are bound to arise as a result of adopting a selective rather than a universal type of plan as the basis for family allowances.
Universality has many great advantages. The women of this country have developed a great respect for family allowances, partly because payment is made directly to

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
them. As a result, even in households where there is very little money available, there is always extra cash which the mother can use to buy necessities for the children, whether in the form of additional clothing or a little extra food on the table.
It is true this method of distribution has given rise to some misgivings in the province of Quebec. There was a measure of resentment, on social grounds, that the money has not been made available to the husband rather than to the wife. I note that the bill before us does not specify who shall receive the money. The various provinces, in operating their plans, presumably will be able to make this decision for themselves.
In support of the legislation which became effective on July 1, 1945, it was argued that the system then adopted would ensure a greater measure of equality of opportunity for all children. It was argued, also, that it would help ensure an adequate income for large families in receipt of social insurance and social assistance payments while avoiding grants which might diminish the incentive to work. Advocates of the bill argued, too, that it would assist in maintaining higher levels of income and employment during the post-war period.
Over the years the government has not seen fit to keep up to date the standards initially set in 1944. At that time children up to six years old received $5, from six to nine years $6, from 10 to 12 years $7, and from 13 to 15 years $8. These rates were changed in 1957 and children up to the age of 10 received $6, and from 10 to 15 $8. In relations to many of the basic costs of both clothing and extras that children require for school, this payment represented considerable assistance to a family yet, as I say, over the years the government has not seen fit to keep the program up to date. The province of Quebec had a similar program to this which was in the form of a school allowance. This resulted in our adding youth allowances to the family benefit program and included children who were attending school and had not yet reached the age of 21.
The white paper indicated there was to be a reduction in family allowance according to the income of the parents. This has been followed to a certain extent by computing the benefits that will now flow to a young person. This has to be considered with the new tax provisions recently passed in Bill C-169. For the low-income families this will be a definite advantage. For the higher income families the advantage will not be so great.
In this regard, when you consider tax accrual you find the following interesting situation. I should like to refer to a study undertaken with regard to bringing into line the deductions that increase as income rises, the benefits that flow from the present scheme and the new proposal in Bill C-170. For example, a family with two children under the age of 10 years whose total income is $3,000 presently receives a family allowance benefit of $96. Under the new act the family will receive a further $120, bringing the total allowance up to $216. No deduction from that sum would be made under Bill C-169, the tax bill, so the whole of the $216 is a benefit to that family.
At the $10,000 level the same family would continue to receive the $96 allowance but there would be a tax deduction of $50.07, which means they get a total net benefit of about $46. At the $25,000 level they would still receive the $96 allowance, and under the new scheme they will receive a total of $328.82, more than $100 over the benefit received by the family earning $3,000. So it is quite true that a family which receives benefits under this act receives more if its total income is low, and the family earning $10,000 will suffer a reduction of $100 more than at present.
Another factor to take into consideration is the cost of operating the plan. Under the present plan a person sent in an application for benefits when a child was born and the following month the benefits commenced. When making an application under the new act for family allowance you have to include a statement of estimated or actual income. Clause 8 provides:
(1)	Where an application for a benefit in respect of a child is made in respect of a current benefit year, the application shall not be approved
(a)	where the parents of the child were resident in Canada for the complete base calendar year, unless a statement of the income of the child's family for that year has been submitted by the parents; or
(b)	where the parents of the child were not resident in Canada for the complete base calendar year, unless a statement of the estimated income of the child's family for the first calendar year thereafter in which the parents reasonably expect to be resident in Canada has been submitted by the parents, in which case the income of the child's family for that calendar year shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
(2)	Where at any time during the base calendar year or during the fourth month of a current benefit year a parent
(a)	ceases to hold an office or employment previously held by him or ceases to carry on a business previously carried on by him, or
(b)	for any other reason suffers a loss or reduction of income,
as a result of which event or occurrence it is reasonable to expect that the income of the family for the calendar year next following the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place will be substantially reduced, the parents may, in such manner and within such time as are prescribed, file a statement of the estimated income of the family for that next following calendar year, in which case the income of the family for that calendar year shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
That is very clear up to that point, but subclause (3) provides:
(3)	Where at any time during the first eleven months of a benefit year, other than the fourth month, or during the eight-month period next before that benefit year a parent
(a)	ceases to hold an office or employment previously held by him or ceases to carry on a business previously carried on by him, or
(b)	for any other reason suffers a loss or reduction of income,
as a result of which event or occurrence-
And so on it goes, Mr. Speaker. The whole of this provision relates to the filing of an application for family allowance. If someone who is called upon to read this act cannot reduce it to plain English, then obviously the poor woman who leaves hospital and wants to make an application on behalf of her newborn child will have considerable difficulty.

I think this illustrates the complexity of the legislation and the difficulty involved in trying to sort out those who will and those who will not be eligible for the family allowance. Of course, every time we produce legislation that is confusing it means there will be a great deal of cost in the administration of the program. It is interesting to note that in the years 1969 and 1970 the administrative cost for family and youth allowances amounted to $11.6 million, or only 1.8 per cent of the total payments. It is estimated the administrative cost will rise sharply, not only because of the complicated provisions in the bill but because of the possibility of several provinces introducing their own allowance scales.
In relation to any legislation I believe there is violent reaction by the general public to having to fill out forms and provide a vast duplication of information to government agencies. Then there is the fact that on occasion this information is a question of interpretation which is subject to change. If a member of a family should obtain employment for a time there would be a change in the family income. If the breadwinner should be sick there would be a change in the family income. Each change, of course, would involve either an overpayment or additional payment which would have to be made in light of the family allowance payment.
Obviously, the administration will be 100 times more complicated than it is in a program involving the payment of a straight grant operated on the basis of age of the child. In my opinion it will be a great deal more expensive to arrive at a calculation as to what the family benefits should be, either under a projected or a base-year income program, than the saving involved in respect of those who really do not need this kind of assistance. I believe it is interesting to note that in some areas the working poor are at a much lower income level than even welfare recipients. The minimum wage in most areas is below what is considered to be the poverty line.
The minimum wage is on an almost uniform basis in the provinces and the welfare structure is based on need, which takes into consideration the size of the family and the type of accommodation it occupies. In many cases the welfare level is much higher than the minimum wage. By looking at a person's income one is really not in a position to make a decision as to whether or not that person is in a better position than someone else to maintain children and pay for their necessities.
I find this situation in respect of the student loans legislation where such a criterion is used. I am thinking particularly of a small store which also has a restaurant in a very small community in my area. The daughter of the people who own this store and restaurant attended university for several years. When she applied for a student loan it was immediately rejected on the basis that the father and mother operated a store. I think it is safe to say-certainly experience has proven this-that in relation to the net income derived from that business the family is living very close to the poverty line as indicated by the welfare structure in the area. This girl eventually was able to obtain a student loan. Originally, however, it was automatically turned down on the basis that her
Family Income Security Plan
mother and father operated a small store and restaurant, which placed them in a certain category.
It seems to me this will be the situation of many young couples who have children and are living considerably beyond their means. It may well be that this government will soon get around this regulation. We certainly have many tables. We have them in respect of income tax and unemployment insurance and now are to have them in respect of family allowances. We will probably have them in respect of most of our health legislation. So, shortly we will have an indication of what the family income should produce in terms of housing. Probably we will be telling people, as we tell them now in the low-income field if they are receiving the old age pension and are living in a rental unit, that they should pay $36 in rent. If the federal government is making a payment through the supplementary benefit program, then obviously the rent would be increased to the maximum of, I believe, $80 and the federal government would pay it. In any case, the decision concerning what type of housing a person will have is made according to his income.
I believe the public is becoming fed up with the government asking how it is spending its money and whether or not it is able to get along with the special benefits. I am sure every member has spoken to old age pensioners who are under this kind of structure asking for supplementary benefits and the government, on examining their total finances, sometimes finds they have over the years purchased war bonds or something of that nature which they have put away for old age, burial or whatever it may be. So long as they have this money they are unable to obtain a reasonable amount of assistance.
I believe we should be working toward less of this type of automated control based on income and should be providing benefits to all those in need. Members of parliament have been receiving a reasonable salary and I am sure most of us have been able to assist our children to attend university. I do not believe we are opposed, although our children may be, to paying for their university education while someone not in our salary category is receiving a government grant or loan of perhaps more money than parents like us who may be considered affluent have made available to our children.
I think the same situation may exist in respect of the family allowance program. There may be young people, and certainly there will be children who will be deprived of some of the benefits we intended them to have when in 1944 we first talked about instituting the family allowance program. Many of our young people have less of an advantage under the new system than they have under the present one.
I hope that after the next election there will be sufficient change so that the government will react to the needs of the people, so that we will make an attempt to get rid of the huge bureaucracy with which the individual must deal and will not pass this type of legislation which provides that assistance is to be given to those who are poor, with no assistance going to those who are rich. This type of legislation means that we establish people in those categories and we enact legislation to keep them there.

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
I hope we will enact legislation providing that when the individual reaches a certain age he is entitled to a certain benefit, legislation providing that when you are born you are entitled to family allowance, not calculated on your parents' ability to pay their way but provided as a right of a newly arrived citizen of Canada.
When members of parliament go out on the hustings and talk to the people of this country I am sure they will find that one of the major complaints is with respect to the morass of detail and information that people have to provide to government. The criteria governing this information are both degrading and divisive.
I believe that this legislation has accomplished in the years of its existence much that we wanted it to accomplish I am sure it has given the opportunity to many poor families to provide a better education for their children. An opportunity has been provided by the family allowance program to buy clothes for children in order to make them acceptable in our society. The family allowance payments have also been spent on medicine and on additional food for poor families. The only disadvantage that has occurred has been not with respect to the form of the demogrant or the tax structure but the fact that the government knows children do not vote. If children had the franchise, then every time we had an election during the last 15 years there would have been an increase in family allowances to match the increases in old age pensions.
Old age pensioners had the vote and governments remembered them. However, after the 1968 election the government had such a huge majority that no increase was given to old age pensioners but a scheme was introduced to assist those in dire need, a totally new program providing a guaranteed income supplement. I suggest that if children were able to vote, Mr. Speaker, we would not have this kind of silly, selectivity-based program.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to say what I think of family allowances in our modern society; to my mind, this is the most important problem in Canadian history because it is the very basis of our society.
Mr. Speaker, the structures and institutions of peoples are undergoing deep transformations these days and our country cannot escape them. These transformations accompany cultural, economic and social evolution, which profoundly influence the political life of our society, especially with regard to the rights and duties of the individual in the exercise of civil liberties and the pursuit of the common good and with regard to the structure of relations between citizens and between the citizen and public powers.
Awareness of human dignity has grown more acute. Efforts must be made to set up a political-judicial order in which the rights of the individual in public life are better protected, while being closely related to present economic and social progress. There is more co-operation and this is likely to guarantee to each and everyone, not only to a privileged few, the true enjoyment of the rights that attach to the human being.
Mr. Speaker, the adoption of a truly human policy implies, above all else, the development of an intimate

sense of justice reinforced by fundamental convictions on the true nature of the political community as an end, the sound exercise and the limits of public authority. Obviously, the political community and public authority find their basis in human nature and therefore stem from an order established by God, although the choice of political regimes and the appointment of its leaders are left to the free will of the citizens.
As for our present concern, Mr. Speaker, what Canadians are asking is a guaranteed minimum income, not a selective plan such as proposed under Bill C-170.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot get over seeing how much they like to take trouble, to complicate things, to multiply problems, to invent new formulas so that people grow increasingly confused about their relationships with their leaders.
Only family allowances were still readily understood by the working population and received every month with no other complication than the proof of existence off citizens. Bill C-170 will now eliminate this worthy feature of family allowances and leave every family wondering and fending with the perennial increases and decreases in benefits they will get from this government as a result of accounting complications, undecipherable for the non-university graduates.
So, Mr. Speaker, instead of speaking of universal or selective programs, why not just call them national, instead of using the big word "universal" which I suggest has no logical meaning here in Canada.
If the allowances plan were called national, applying to the whole territory of Canada, it would definitely be known that it extends to Canadians of all the provinces and territories of our country. But what does "universal" mean, actually? And what about "selective"? Another lovely gem, which only further complicates concertation involving the guaranteed family income.
So, when reading the comments of the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) as they appear on page 1131 of Hansard for March 24, 1972, I feel humiliated in my pride as a Canadian citizen and ask that this House, seeing to what extent this study of family allowances and security of family income is linked with concern over lack of money for the family, the children, the human person in need and the population in general, take some action.
Mr. Speaker, when it is a matter of doubling, tripling the income of corporations, banks and big institutions, there is no limit to our ambitions, skills and possibilities. Crown corporations are easily created with stock amounting to $2 billion. A bill is merely brought forward in the House of Commons and everything runs smoothly. But when it is a matter of the children of the country, the Minister of National Health-why not universal health-and Welfare had this to say, which I quote from the second column of page 1131 of Hansard for March 24:
Payments per child of $72 to $120 a year, in essence the level of payments which our present family allowance program provides, cannot come near the annual cost of maintaining a child.
March 28, 1972

I keep quoting:
One must take into account that current coverage involves almost 7 million children-
We see the tremendous expenditures involved when we start to double the rates and benefits under the present family allowances if we just double them and make them universal.
And so, Mr. Speaker, the whole speech of the hon. minister on family allowances reveals his fear of running short of money to give a decent life to Canadian children out of the incalculable resources that Providence has bestowed upon this country.
Mr. Speaker, it bears repeating over again that this approach to family income security and personal and family allowances is terribly depressing and even ridiculous on the part of our most intelligent people in parliament, who are merely trying to summarize the Canadian government's policy expressed in the now famous white paper, published a year ago following exhaustive university, administrative and legislative research by our national and provincial elite. The results are really depressing, ridiculous and discouraging. To all who are good at arithmetic, I am tempted to give a little lesson.
I am going to quote this other sentence of the Minister of Health and Welfare, which is also on page 1133 of Hansard:
By this measure the government will be committing $820 million to the FISP proposals, a sizeable increase over the amount now expended on family allowances . . . roughly $650 million.
How about that? One hundred and seventy million more. This-$170 million more for seven million children up to 17 years of age inclusively, which is, a third of the population-is a crushing burden for Canada, whose national product-not universal, mind, but national-was from $92 billion to $95 billion in 1971 and 1972, and will be over $100 billion in 1972-73.
Can you imagine? To have been afraid to increase allowances in respect of children, of students under 18 years of age, by $170 million when the national product is going to increase by over $8 billion in the coming year. I will, therefore, urge the minister to make the calculation and stop making a fool of himself on behalf of all learned Canadians.
Does the minister not understand that an increase of $170 million on an extra production of $8 billion in Canada for next year is only a peanut in a wheat field? Where does he get his proportions and percentages?
An amount of $820 million out of $100 billion, that is not even one per cent. We should stop making fools of ourselves, stop mocking the people who are beginning to see through this play on figures, because the game is the same with millions as it is with dollars and cents. The percentages, the proportions are the same whether you figure out millions or billions, cents or dollars.
So, the minister will finally understand without need for further comments. He himself said, as reported on page 1131 of Hansard for March 24, 1972, and I quote:
-family allowances have lost their effectiveness over the years, as benefits have remained almost unchanged since their inception despite sharp increases in the cost of living.
I say to the minister that this sentence would have more strength and informative value if we made a calculation
Family Income Security Plan
of percentages and proportions from the beginning, or from 1945.
However, the national production amounted to only $12 billion in 1944-45. In 1971, it was $92 billion and it will increase to $100 billion in 1972.
In 1944, the basic salary for MP's was $4,000; it is now $26,000 which is seven times more. However, family allowances have remained the same. We are the ones to decide, according to our judgment and our knowledge.
The income for MP's, judges, ministers, university graduates, accountants and economists is based on the cost of living, proportionately to the national production, whereas for children who make up one third of the population, we are still maintaining the rates in effect in 194445 whence Canada's production was $12 billion, that is seven or eight times less than today.
We are now in 1972. Mr. Speaker, I could quote a dozen tables which show quite clearly the lack of responsibility or understanding of our governing and thinking elite concerning proportions, percentages, the sharing of income and the purchasing power at the various levels of population.
I have no intention of needlessly annoying hon. members by striking a discordant note. I would rather at any time play a harmonious tune which has to do with the economic balance that ought to prevail in Canada under the auspices of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, every Canadian wishes and heartily strives for understanding, economic balance in the country at every level of the population. Nobody wants to see the disharmony and the lack of balance which prevail today because of inflation, unemployment and poverty.
However, this correction must be made in our national economy. No other authority but the one at the national level, the Parliament of Canada, is in a position to administer our national economy.
What does this parliament consist of? The 264 members elected by the people on June 25, 1968, among whom we notice thirty-odd ministers and as many parliamentary secretaries, all the Liberals responsible for legislation with the support of members of the various opposition parties also elected by the Canadian people, as well as 102 senators.
It does seem therefore that on such an important issue as the security of family income, all members and ministers elected by the people of Canada, all equally interested in the well-being of nearly 23 million Canadians, should get together regarding this matter, the most important economic question, that is the security of family and personal income, which should be granted to citizens from the enormous national and natural resources that we own, with the co-operation of capital and labour of adult citizens and producers.
If only we could at long last become aware of the importance of the life of the citizens, as opposed to that of capital and the work of those who contribute to national production, we would at least have taken an initial and direct step towards economic harmony, towards balance between the various segments of our national economy.

March 28, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
We could at long last hope to see an end to inflation, unemployment, poverty.
But all that requires recognition of the prime objective of all government and parliament activity-guaranteeing the survival and the income of every citizen. The life of the human being, that is the first objective of all government administration. Human life must take precedence over the primacy of capital or labour because, without human life, where would capital or labour be?
If we have provided to such an extent for the protection of capital, guaranteed income or labour, why should we not afford as much or even more protection to human life, even that of the unemployed or the penniless? Such is the main object of any administration or any efficient legislation of this parliament or this government of Canada. This is the question which should be the main concern of the ministers and elected representatives of Canadians who are now close to 23 million and who are entitled to live before being entitled to employment or capital.
If capital does exist apart from the human being, if labour does exist as an expression of the human being, life is the very basis of that human being and the basis of his labour or capital. Without life there cannot be any capital nor labour for any citizen.
Therefore that life must be our first goal when we administer the economy of our country in the same way as that life is the first expression of the existence of every living citizen, even before he is able to work, even before he is able to own some capital. Life comes first, labour and capital follow suit. Is it really that order we follow in our administrative priorities? It is not surprising that the economy is out of balance, that capital is at grips with inflation, that labour suffers from all kinds of unemployment and that the life of the citizen is threatened by the harassing existence of shameful and depressing poverty.
Mr. Speaker, at long last here is that famous Bill C-170 on family income security. Are we going to deal with it in the same way as with all other major economic bills, including the Bank Act, the tax reform and the Unemployment Insurance Act, when all our efforts only resulted in providing greater sources of guaranteed income for capital, in triggering at the same time and as a consequence the increase in prices, taxes, all things that increase the cost of living, even for all the citizens who have no work and no capital, no source of guaranteed personal income, neither through work nor through capital?
This is why, the more we step forward, the more we go backward in dealing with inflation, unemployment and poverty. It is very simple. We take the wrong approach. We see things upside down. We seek to protect capital and work before protecting the life of the people of this country. Everything is mixed up in our minds. We think we are going up when in fact we are going down.
This is why capital becomes more and more important at the expense of work which is given less and less value, at the expense of personal incomes which are taxed more than ever, at the expense of the life of those out of work, without capital who are becoming poorer and poorer because the cost of living is going up, even for those who

are too young, too old or too sick or unable to eke out a livelihood through their work or their capital.
Are we forgetting that life is the prime source of personal income, that before working or owning capital, each and every living citizen, whether he is a child, a student, an adult or an older person, has a right to live from the first moment of his existence to the last beat of his heart?
Nevertheless, the tremendous research work done by this government since it gained power has made us conscious of the economic situation in our country, Canadian companies, families and each and every citizen of this country.
Mr. Speaker, the individuals, the families and the companies, whether private or public, are what is being administered in Canada under the unique leadership of the government which is comprised of 264 members of parliament elected by over 22 million Canadians. In 1972, national output will reach $100 bil'ion, more than $4,500 per person on the average, which represents $22,500 for a family of five. We are rich and we live poorly. All this can be corrected through a minor readjustment in guaranteed personal income, in the right to essential things for each family of this country according to the decision we can take, we the members of parliament elected by the people for a term of five years legally ending in mid-July 1973.
That decision rests upon us. No other Canadian citizen can be held responsible for that decision. Each and every one had the opportunity of expressing his opinion thanks to the many inquiries held by royal commissions over the past ten years, and to studies of task forces and debates on white papers. Time has come for action, legislation, administration, the new economic order we want to establish and which is the responsibility of all of us, ministers and members.
The president of the Royal Bank of Canada, the chairmen of many companies with assets of more than $40 billion, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Donald MacDonald, with his two million union members, bishops, cardinals and the Pope, none of them can vote for or against family income security. Here, in Parliament, not even bishops, cardinals or the Queen of England could vote for or against guaranteed personal income. Therefore, it is our duty and our exclusive and complete privilege to make a decision on that urgent matter.
In order to finish its task and to establish a just society in a unique and united Canada, to create a permanent guaranteed family income for every one and for each Canadian family, for every home, apartment, residence or slum dweller in Canada, within our present monetary, economic and political and capitalist framework in our better understood free enterprise system, the present majority government has one full year left. It is entirely responsible for its decisions once opposition members have been allowed to express their personal opinions on this all important subject for the future of Canada.
If capital is treated fairly in corporations of all kinds, if work is respected by unions, big or small, the fact remains that the rights of each citizen must be considered and protected unconditionally and very closely through Bill C-170 on which we cannot vote without due reflection.
March 28, 1972

For the 22 million Canadians, there must be 22 million guaranteed incomes whether through capital or work or the basic personal rights of citizens who have no work nor money.
Mr. Speaker, since personal capital earns a guaranteed interest set by contract, since personal labour deserve a guaranteed salary established through contracts, therefore each dependent citizen deserves a guaranteed minimum by contract. This is what we should accomplish through Bill C-170.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, out of a national product of $100 billion which, on the average, amounts to $4,500 for each person or $22,500 for each family of five, there is nothing preventing us from legislating on a personal guaranteed minimum as follows: family allowances for all children up to age 10 for those aged 10 to 17, for all adults between 18 and 59 and for all pensioners aged 60 or more.
This table shows the amounts paid to each citizen in every family where the breadwinner earns an income through his work or his capital. For those families or single persons who do not earn any income through work or capital, an additional premium for motherhood, for guidance or for loneliness will be automatically added to the guaranteed personal income. As regards contributions, the program is selective and national. It is a national program in that it does not neglect anyone. It is an easily assessable national program calculated on the basis of $1 a day, or $30 a month, which is within the understanding of most Canadian families, whatever their level of education. Once the principles are recognized, the logical means must also be accepted.
Let us take time to ponder this table which is quite easy to grasp and think of all the citizens who have a right to live proportionately to our national production, year after year, before individuals and prosperous corporations can accumulate large amounts of capital for the years to come. Before capitalizing too much there must be enough consumption, Mr. Speaker.
I am well aware that it is impossible to express one's ideas in a few sentences, but this is enough to stimulate the curiosity of each one of us. I can give you more details, if you wish.
As regards production, Mr. Speaker, we should add an additional $12 to 16 billion for the guaranteed security of each citizen. It is very simple: we could draw from production itself an amount of $12 to 15 billion to be added to insufficient consumption; this amount would be levied on extravagant and inflationary capitalization, and would bring about increased purchasing power and, at the same time, lower prices and taxes; it would also stem inflation while maintaining the availability of $24 to 30 billion for capitalization, development and progress in Canada. This still gives an average-

You cannot say it all in a few paragraphs, or answer in advance all the objections which are a cause of anxiety to Canadians who may feel affected by this correction of our national economy, but let us think right now of the wellbeing which could be brought to every Canadian home and to every sector of the economy by this injection of several billions of dollars distributed at the rate of $1 a day per child, about $60 a month for students, and around $90 or $150 for unemployed adults with no capital.
Besides, only members of parliament in Canada have the necessary legislative responsibility and authority to so restore the national economic balance, to eliminate inflation, unemployment and poverty in the normal framework of our monetary, economic and political system.
Mr. Speaker, there are many things we could say. I should like to quote from a speech published in the October 8, 1971 edition of Le Devoir.
Having spoken about the Belgian family allowances system, which is a progressive allowance system, Mr. Vermeire expressed concern about the new family allowances schemes proposed by Canada and the province of Quebec. He said: "It seems they wish to grant them only below a definite income ceiling, a definite standard of living. It is the opposite of what it should be. Family allowances are not social welfare but a question of horizontal justice.
We could quote hundreds of similar texts stating that the plan now proposed by the government is unacceptable in such a wealthy country as ours, a country where we have only resources to distribute. Instead of doing so, we are doling this money out, to those who really need it, those who are the real consumers in our society. The family is society's greatest consumer and we need such consumers in Canada. Why then should we deprive our families? They represent the most important consumers in Canada.
The family today has all kinds of needs, unsatisfied needs. And to meet them, our production, which is abundant, is there to serve, to meet to satisfy, the needs of Canadians.
It is therefore up to us to so organize our economy that this abundance be distributed to those who need it, to those who are now deprived in our country, who could consume much more than they do now.

It is up to us to supply them with economic means, give them economic security, the surplus we have in Canada and see that this surplus meets every need. Every human being has his needs and they should all be met in a truly just administration, truly healthy and truly loyal.

Mr. Speaker, the minister the other day almost popped his buttons, in a literal fashion, with pride at what this government has done in connection with what he claims to be an improvement of the income security program. The hon. member will have the right to make his own speech. If it is felt that there has to be some change, I would have thought it far simpler and in fact far more equitable to bring any family allowance scheme within taxable income so that any family allowance payment received would be taxed at the marginal rate applicable to that particular taxpayer.
Under this bill we are going to have a different arrangement, and what a bureaucratic nightmare it is! Family allowance will be based on family income for the first time. There are many provisions in the Income Tax Act that deny family income; family income has to be kept separate. But for the purposes of this bill the income is joined. That is the first point.
In addition, during the first year income will be estimated during the base revenue year, which is the previous year, and may bear no relationship to the income in the year in question. Take the case, for example, of a married woman who is working, who becomes pregnant, has her child and ceases to work during the year that follows while the child is still small. She has to base her claim for family allowance for her child on the revenue of herself and her husband for the previous year when she was working. In other words, her family allowance payment will be less than it should be because of the required overstatement of her earnings.
Then, take the case of the husband who is overpaid during a given year because his actual earnings are greater than his estimated earnings. Who is going to make the recovery? Who is going to audit that return? There are provisions in the bill regarding repayments and adjustments, but all of these items call for paperwork on the part of the individual recipient of family allowance as well as on the part of the control branch of the government. Again, it would have been far simpler to take it in as part of income and tax it according to that person's income.

Another point is this. Under the Income Tax Act which we passed late last year there is provision for the payment of child-care allowance before determination of taxable income. The expense of caring for a child has now been introduced into the concept of earning an income. That was accepted in the case of working parents or single parents. IMMIGRATION-COMPLAINTS BY TORONTO POLICE ABOUT DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING DEPORTATION ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has many immigrants. In this century Canada has admitted approximately three million immigrants to its shores.
March 28, 1972

These people from various countries who have settled here have contributed significantly to our growth and to our development in every field.
In March, 1967, the government introduced the Immigration Appeal Board Act. It was passed by Parliament and was intended to remove ministerial discretion in the great majority of deportation cases and allow a court set up under the statute to deal with appeals from deportation. Since the new immigration regulations of September, 1967, which instituted an assessment system and removed geographical limitations and other discriminatory factors, an unexpected and unprecedented number of applications by people wishing to settle in Canada has been received by Canadian immigration authorities.
These potential immigrants saw Canada, with its freedom, its beauty, richness and great potential, as the best place in the world in which to live. Consequently, immigration offices both at home and abroad have been flooded with many applications. Unfortunately, since many visitors to Canada have decided to stay and ask for landed immigrant status the processing of these applications in Canada has become very complex and long. When rejected by immigration officials applicants have the right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board. Today I learned that there is a backlog of about 7,000 cases involving appeals from deportation orders. These cases are awaiting decisions by the Immigration Appeal Board.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-COMPLAINTS BY TORONTO POLICE ABOUT DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING DEPORTATION ORDERS
speechtext: They are all going to lose, too.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-COMPLAINTS BY TORONTO POLICE ABOUT DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING DEPORTATION ORDERS
speechtext: Apart from these people there are in this country many so-called deserters, draft-dodgers and others who have drifted to Canada from the United States. They have compounded the problem. I have received many representations from my constituents and have also been in contact with people concerned, especially in Toronto, about this matter. These people tell me that waiting two or three years to be heard involves great hardship for them. That is why I think the Immigration Appeal Board Act should be amended to provide for at least double the number of Immigration Appeal Board officials who could hear this great backlog of cases.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-COMPLAINTS BY TORONTO POLICE ABOUT DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING DEPORTATION ORDERS
speechtext: Notice who is on the board now: they are ex-members of the Liberal party.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-COMPLAINTS BY TORONTO POLICE ABOUT DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING DEPORTATION ORDERS
speechtext:
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the difficulty has been compounded by fugitives or people wanted by the police. People like that have come to this country and have created problems for our police forces and the police forces of other countries who are seeking them. The Toronto police department, especially, has complained about problems in this regard. They want amendments made to the act and procedures in immigration offices, especially in Toronto, improved in order that they can deal with these cases swiftly and justly. Tonight, I hope that I will be given a reassuring answer by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, (Mr. Perrault) as to whether there is in the making any policy which will help solve this complex problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION-COMPLAINTS BY TORONTO POLICE ABOUT DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING DEPORTATION ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have investigated the circumstances of the issue raised by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) with respect to general immigration policy and charges made by a member of the Toronto police department to the effect that recourse to extradition proceedings has to be made in removing from Canada unwanted criminals, rather than deportation proceedings, because of what was quoted as ineptitude and delays on the department's part in carrying out its responsibilities. In our view this is a completely unfair and unfounded charge.
As all hon. members know, while there are delays in the holding of certain immigration inquiries for people not able to comply with our laws, this is not the case in so far as persons arrested under the provisions of the Immigration Act, who are known and wanted fugitives from justice, are concerned. The Immigration Act is very explicit in indicating that such proceedings under the Immigration Act must be taken immediately, and this is being done. Persons so arrested and ordered deported do, however, have the right of appeal against their deportation to the independent Immigration Appeal Board.
It is also a known fact that this independent board is faced with a substantial backlog which is resulting in delays in the hearing of appeals. Indeed, the former minister of manpower and immigration tabled a report to the government by an eminent legal authority, Mr. Joseph Sedgwick, some time ago on this situation and subsequently indicated on several occasions in this House that measures were being examined to attempt to reduce the total time lapse between the ordering of deportation and its implementation. Just as soon as it is possible to accomplish this, I assure the House that it will be done. In the meantime, police authorities are of course free to choose the alternate extradition method if they consider it more expeditious.

PUBLIC SERVICE-REQUEST FOR INFORMATION ON RECOMMENDATIONS RESPECTING STAFF RELATIONS ACT AND TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 7, in response to my question about the Bryden report, the President of the Privy Council Mr. MacEachen), informed me that it was not his intention to table this report or to take legislative action on it at this session of Parliament. Today, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), he reiterated this stand.
This fresh questioning was undoubtedly triggered by the fact that both the executive director of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada and the president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada recently have written strong letters to the government demanding publication of the Bryden report. It took several months to prepare this document at the taxpayers' expense a year ago. Time and care went into its preparation. All staff associations submitted extensive briefs which were made public.
However, the brief submitted by Treasury Board has been kept secret. Why? What does it contain that the
25104-20?

March 28, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
government fears to release at this time? What does the Bryden report include in the way of recommendations that the government is so anxious to keep from the light of day? Is the government afraid that if the report is released the public will demand that action be taken in this session of parliament, before an election? Why is the government determined not to trust either the public service or the public with the facts and recommendations coritained in the report?
This matter involves a quarter of a million federal public servants. With their families they number approximately a million Canadians, about one in twenty of the population. Why should all these people be kept up against a blank wall indefinitely? Changing conditions over the past few years have resulted in amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act which were not only desirable but vitally necessary. The field of subjects included in collective bargaining needs to be widened to include such matters as classification and superannuation.
The legislation as it stands actually favours strike action as a solution of deadlocks because so few matters can now be dealt with by arbitration. But even this procedure is very limited and needs amendment so as to make provision for the services of an independent adjudicator. These are only a few of the more urgent amendments required.
Before the Public Service Staff Relations Act was passed some years ago, the Heeney report was prepared and tabled in Parliament. Now that the act needs amendment, why cannot the Bryden report be tabled in its turn? The answer may lie in the different attitudes of government toward the public service then and now. It used to be considered unsporting for a minister publicly to attack a civil servant. Now we hear a minister publicly branding a member of his staff as stupid, without giving him any opportunity of defending himself.
It would be difficult to imagine Prime Minister Pearson, when asked about collective bargaining in the public service, replying that the staff associations and unions appeared to be suffering from "insufficiency of thought" in connection with the problems arising from public staff relations, and that they were not helping the government to find better solutions. But we hear this from our present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whose government refuses to release a report which is vital to the processes of collective bargaining in the public service. What the government appears to suffer from as far as the Bryden report is concerned is insufficiency of action.

I have had more chances than I am accustomed to in one day. No one questions the importance of the subject of collective bargaining in the public service or of the importance of collective bargaining generally. Certainly, we do not question the importance of the study in that regard or the importance in the minds of the
(Mrs. Maclnnis.]
Canadian people of the questions which have been raised by the hon. member. But nothing the hon. member has said changes the situation respecting the general picture as to the disposition of studies prepared for the confidential use of the government.
The time to decide about the release of these documents is when a study is being prepared, because the decision will affect the manner in which it is conducted and the way in which the report is compiled. It would not be good enough to tell the people who have conducted such a study, after it had been prepared, that one had changed one's mind on the question of releasing it. If a specific undertaking has been given, the people who have prepared the study are entitled to rely on consistency of thought in that regard.
Whether or not the hon. member agrees with what was done, the fact is that those were the terms under which the study was prepared and those are the terms in which the government views the situation at the present time. And, as has been already stated by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), this is a document intended for the confidential use of the government and will not be tabled. I can only confirm that legislative action on the basis of that study is not contemplated during the present session. Those are the only remarks I have to make on the subject at this time.

FINANCE-POSSIBLE REDEMPTION OF THREE PER CENT PERPETUAL BONDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 21 I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) with reference to the government's plans, if any, to redeem the so-called perpetual bond issue put out in 1936. To set the record straight, at that time, on a point of order, I suggested the minister had not answered my correspondence on two occasions. I want it to be clear that I was referring to only one letter of September 20 which concerned the matter of criminal law reform. It was only one letter that he did not answer with regard to the question I asked him on March 21.
The minister has since replied, though to my way of thinking in a most unsatisfactory manner. It seems obvious to me that a government which can devise such a cumbersome and complex tax reform bill as we saw recently could certainly devise a plan which would be equitable to those who in 1936 invested to the tune of $55 million in the future of this country and who have since seen their investment eroded to the point at which it is almost a joke.
I doubt very much if the 1936 perpetual bonds could be sold for more than $50 at the most, perhaps for only $40 per $100 of their par value. To me this is nothing less than a national disgrace. It is hardly creditable for a country such as Canada, which purports to be one of the world's leading financial nations, to put out an official government issue which compares with some of the Russian or Chinese bonds issued early in the nineteenth century.
March 28, 1972

It is strange to me that the Minister of Finance cannot recognize the hardship inflicted upon Canadians who have been holding these bonds which are now returning about 3.1 per cent in interest. Surely the Minister of Finance could devise some plan, based on random serial numbers or otherwise, which would alleviate the hardship which these investors have encountered since 1936. That is about the year in which I was born, Mr. Speaker. I realize I have depreciated a great deal since that time, but not as much as these bonds, I suggest.
This is a matter of concern. Surely a country's bonds are a measure of its integrity. As a Canadian and a member of parliament I am embarrassed to think that a bond issue involving some $50 million should have earned such an ill reputation on the bond market that it should have sunk to its present level. It seems to me, despite the minister's comments in page 2 of his letter to me, that he should recognize that redemption of these bonds has become a matter of national conscience.
It may well be said that to redeem these bonds would be to create a precedent which would suggest to anyone with an investment, government or otherwise, that something should be done to make certain that their investment is protected. This is not the case. When a government guarantees that bonds will be redeemable at par, a person has fair warning when they buy the bonds. Here we have a bond issue and there is no guarantee when they will be redeemed. As far as the people who are unfortunate enough to hold the bonds are concerned, they have something that is worth practically nothing. It is true that they could perhaps get $40 or $50 for these bonds, but there is no guarantee that they will get their money back at any particular time. The very stigma attached to these bonds should make them an embarrassment to a country such as Canada.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
It seems to me that all the minister has to do is accept the fact that these bonds are unique both in terms of their perpetual nature and their low yield. Does the minister not think that these bonds deserve special treatment, contrary to the observation in his letter to me? I suggest that they do, that this is an important enough issue for the Minister of Finance to address himself to it immediately and give very real thought to correcting what is a blot on the financial reputation and record of this or any government.
Mr. ]udd Buchanan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the situation clarified regarding the two letters. We were able to locate only the one letter dealing with this subject, but I will be happy to check into the previous letter, which I gather dealt with another subject, and see just what the situation is.
As for the subject raised by the hon. member, the concern is that these perpetual bonds are marketable and that their price is determined in the bond market. In his letter the minister indicated that he was aware that a number of persons who were holders of these bonds could ill afford the capital loss that would be involved in selling at current market prices.
A good deal of consideration has been given to this problem, including, as suggested by the hon. member, recalling these bonds on the basis of random serial numbers. Unfortunately, all such proposals carried with them the implication of protecting investors in marketable securities from the vagaries of the market. To accept this principle, even in circumstances designed to alleviate hardship, would in the opinion of the minister lead, quite understandably, to demands for similar treatment by all other investors in government of Canada marketable securities selling below their issue price. In these circumstances it was felt that this is not an undertaking into which the government would like to launch itself.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.21 p.m.

Wednesday, March 29, 1972
